catalog_quote: Primary stress placement in Takia is unusual in that it is related to vowel height. Within a word (which includes affixes but not clitics), primary stress falls by default on the final syllable: tama-n [ta'man] father-3SG 'her/his father'; u-sol [u'sol] 2SG-flee 'you fled'; i-fn-o [ifu'no] 3SG-hit-2SG 's/he hit you'; t-gi-o [tigi'o] 1INC:PL-call-2SG 'we called you'. However, it occurs on an earlier syllable if that syllable's vowel is lower than the vowel(s) of any succeeding syllables: nanu-n ['nanun] child-3SG 'her/his child'; ŋa-sol ['ŋasol] 1SG-flee 'I fled'. ... Thus the lexical forms of [kiri'ŋen] and [suku'lon] above are /krŋén/ and /sklón/ (for readability's sake I use an acute accent to mark stress, even though this is redundant).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Primary stress placement in Takia is unusual in that it is related to vowel height. Within a word (which includes affixes but not clitics), primary stress falls by default on the final syllable: tama-n [ta'man] father-3SG 'her/his father'; u-sol [u'sol] 2SG-flee 'you fled'; i-fn-o [ifu'no] 3SG-hit-2SG 's/he hit you'; t-gi-o [tigi'o] 1INC:PL-call-2SG 'we called you'. However, it occurs on an earlier syllable if that syllable's vowel is lower than the vowel(s) of any succeeding syllables: nanu-n ['nanun] child-3SG 'her/his child'; ŋa-sol ['ŋasol] 1SG-flee 'I fled'.
new_statements.citation: Ross, Malcolm. 2002. Takia. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds.), The Oceanic Languages, 216-248. Richmond: Curzon.
new_statements.locator: §1.3 'Stress and syllabification', p. 218 (archive.org PDF p. 235); secondary stress pp. 218-220; clitics/formative p. 221
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (941 pp, archive.org item 'crowley-.-the-oceanic-languages', community upload dated 2011 reprint) and rendered/ran extracted text on PDF pp. 233-239 (= printed 216-222), plus the saved page image. Printed p. 218, §1.3 'Stress and syllabification', reads exactly as quoted: 'Primary stress placement in Takia is unusual in that it is related to vowel height. Within a word (which includes affixes but not clitics), primary stress falls by default on the final syllable: [table: tama-n [ta'man] father-3SG 'her/his father'; u-sol [u'sol] 2SG-flee 'you fled'; i-fn-o [ifu'no] 3SG-hit-2SG 's/he hit you'; t-gi-o [tigi'o] 1INC:PL-call-2SG 'we called you'] However, it occurs on an earlier syllable…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default final stress within the phonological word (root plus affixes), overridden by vowel height: primary stress goes to the leftmost syllable whose vowel is strictly lower (more sonorous: a > e,o > i,u) than the vowels of every following syllable; with equal or rising vowel height the last syllable wins (ta'man, u'sol, ifu'no) while a lower earlier vowel attracts it ('nanun, 'ŋasol). Many pre-tonic [i]/[u] are non-lexical inserted vowels (lexical /krŋen/ -> [kiri'ŋen]) and do not affect placement; Ross notes stress is 'redundant' (predictable) and marks it only for readability. Not syllable-weight-based in the usual sense: the 'weight' is vowel sonority, so a fixed: final syllable-with-sonority-override reading is equally defensible.
new_statements.secondary_stress: After the primary ('part B'): if two or three syllables follow, a secondary stress falls on the second syllable after the primary regardless of vowel (kanaorig [ka.'na.o.ˌrig] 'earthquake'), 'often hardly perceptible'. Before the primary ('part A'): with two or more preceding syllables, secondary stress falls on any (C)VC syllable or any syllable with /a/, otherwise on every second syllable leftward from the primary (i-fn-o [ˌi.fu.'no]; kumatiao [ku.ˌma.ti.'a.o]); /a/ syllables in part A are always secondarily stressed, producing adjacent stressed syllables (tama-n [ˌta.'man]), optionally reduced in words of three or more syllables; with three or more /a/ syllables in a row one unpredictably loses its stress and vowel (wananan [ˌwa.ˌna.'nan] ~ [ˌwan.'nan]). Unstressed vowels may reduce to [ə].
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics and the derivational formative /-a-/ are never stressed and are excluded from stress assignment (p. 221: /ai-a-n/ 'hipbone' ['ayan] keeps stress on the initial vowel); an optional (a) in some pronoun forms is 'treated as non-existent for stress assignment purposes' (p. 222); a small class of exceptions arises from vowel prothesis before initial /r/ (p. 219). Ross states the 2002 account differs 'significantly' from his 1995 CAD sketch and that the trigger-vowel/stress relationship claimed there is irrelevant ('Waters, contra Ross 1995').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word = root + affixes, excluding clitics (phrase-attached) and the formative. Data are from the coastal dialect recorded at Rigen village, south Karkar Island, 1987-88 (consultant Mait Kilil); Ross says the phonology is the same in all dialects apart from the inland /l/-/r/ merger, but phonetic realisation and part-A syllabification vary between dialects and tokens. The example lists in the quote are tabular in the original (form / phonetic / gloss / translation columns) and have been run together with semicolons.
new_statements.identity_note: Ross 2002 describes the coastal Takia dialect of Rigen village (southern Karkar Island), stating the phonology is otherwise uniform across dialects (inland dialects merge /l/ and /r/). Glottolog taki1248 has no dialect glottocodes; the mainland 'Megiar/Sarang' varieties listed under Takia in the hh bibliography are not covered by the stress description. The SIL OPD (Waters 1992) covers Karkar and Bagabag with no dialect split for phonology.

new_statements.quote: The survey excludes very uncommon patterns, like regular antepenultimate stress in the Polynesian Outlier Ifira-Mele (Clark TOL), or languages like Takia (North New Guinea) where, although primary stress occurs by default on final syllable, it occurs on a nonfinal syllable if the vowel of that syllable is lower than the vowel(s) in syllable(s) following it (Ross TOL).
new_statements.citation: Lynch, John (2000). Reconstructing Proto-Oceanic Stress. Oceanic Linguistics 39(1): 53–82.
new_statements.locator: p. 58 (PDF p. 6), section 3 'Proto-Oceanic stress regimes: a brief survey', paragraph introducing the survey
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 30-page ProQuest image scan, extracted text gives no text). Rendered PDF p. 6 myself (running head '58 OCEANIC LINGUISTICS, VOL. 39, NO. 1') and read the page image: section 3 'PROTO-OCEANIC STRESS REGIMES: A BRIEF SURVEY', third paragraph, reads exactly 'The survey excludes very uncommon patterns, like regular antepenultimate stress in the Polynesian Outlier Ifira-Mele (Clark TOL), or languages like Takia (North New Guinea) where, although primary stress occurs by default on final syllable, it occurs on a nonfinal syllable if the vowel of that syllable is lower than the vowel(s) in syllable(s) following it (Ross TOL).' Verbatim match (TOL is small caps in print). Same page, first paragraph…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statement from Ross 2002 (default final stress, overridden by vowel height); Lynch is citing that very sketch (Ross TOL), so it is not independent evidence. Relative to the catalog record (classification segmental, rule empty) it supplies the rule in one sentence, but adds nothing that Ross 2002 does not already give in more detail (examples, secondary stress, clitic domain).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the final syllable by default, but is pulled to a nonfinal syllable whose vowel is lower (more sonorous) than the vowel(s) of the syllable(s) after it, i.e. vowel-height (sonority) sensitive stress with a final default. Lynch treats this as a very uncommon Oceanic pattern and explicitly leaves Takia out of his survey and his reconstruction; the statement is second-hand, attributed to Ross's sketch in The Oceanic Languages (Ross 2002).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Takia. Lynch states on the same page that he 'will generally ignore secondary stress throughout this paper' and deals almost exclusively with word-level stress.
new_statements.exceptions: The only exception stated is the rule itself: nonfinal placement when a nonfinal vowel is lower than the following vowel(s). No further exceptions, clitic or affix behaviour, or examples are given for Takia; the language is mentioned only this once in the whole article (checked the scanned text for Takia, Bel, Karkar).
new_statements.identity_note: Lynch names the language only as 'Takia (North New Guinea)', with no dialect specified; the description is Ross's, which in the catalog is Ross 2002 (Takia of Karkar Island).

sources.note: Primary stress falls by default on the final syllable of the phonological word (root+affixes, not clitics), but moves to an earlier syllable whose vowel is lower than all following vowels; detailed secondary-stress rules for the syllables before ('part A') and after ('part B') the primary stress; clitics and the formative -a- are never stressed. Ross says this account is 'significantly different from the one in Ross (1995)'.
